prompt: Which of these is a numerical setting that you can converge?

options.why: More points give a result that stops changing, so the mesh converges.
Tempting, but a different functional is a different model, not a finer version of the same one.

options.text: The value of U in DFT+U
options.why: Tempting, but U changes the physics you ask about; it does not converge to a limit.

hints: Which choice gives a result that stops changing as you improve it?
Functionals and U are model choices.

prompt: What does it mean that a series is converged at one setting, in the strict form this site uses?

options.text: Every later setting differs from it by no more than the tolerance
options.why: This avoids calling a flat spot in the middle of a curve converged.

options.text: The next setting differs from it by no more than the tolerance
options.why: Tempting, but a flat spot can fool this weaker test.

options.text: The last setting has the lowest energy
options.why: Tempting, but the lowest value says nothing about whether the curve has levelled off.

hints: Think about a curve that is flat for two points and then falls again.
Which rule looks at all later points?

prompt: What tolerance, in meV per atom, does the author's handbook use for the total energy?
hints: It is a round number.
It is the default of the convergence plotter.

prompt: Which should you write next to a reported energy so that others can judge it?

options.why: The cutoff controls the basis size, so it belongs next to the number.
The mesh decides the Brillouin-zone sampling error.
They set how far the smeared energy is from the zero-smearing one.
Tempting, but the machine does not change the converged result.

hints: Which settings change the number?
Report both ENCUT and the mesh at least.

prompt: In a convergence test you change two settings between runs. What is the main problem?

options.text: You cannot tell which setting moved the result
options.why: Each test should have one moving part.
Tempting, but VASP runs fine; the trouble is in interpreting the curve.
Tempting, but the sign of the energy is unrelated to how many settings changed.

hints: What is the purpose of keeping the others fixed?
Think about reading the curve afterwards.

prompt: Where do you read ENMAX, the recommended cutoff, and which value do you use for a mixed-species cell?

options.text: In each POTCAR; the largest one
options.why: The hardest species sets the basis you need.
Tempting, but POSCAR holds the structure, not cutoffs, and the smallest would under-describe the hardest species.
Tempting, but KPOINTS holds the mesh only.

hints: Which file comes from the pseudopotential library?
`grep ENMAX POTCAR`.

prompt: The series generator is given ENMAX = 400 eV. How many ENCUT values does its default series contain (400 up to 700 eV in 50 eV steps)?
hints: Count 400, 450, 500 and so on.
The end is the first multiple of 50 at or above 1.75 times ENMAX.

prompt: What stays fixed in an ENCUT convergence series?

options.text: The structure, the k-mesh and the smearing
options.why: Only ENCUT may change, or the curve mixes effects.

options.text: The number of electronic steps only
options.why: Tempting, but the mesh and structure must be fixed as well.

options.text: Nothing; each run uses its own best settings
options.why: Tempting, but that makes the runs incomparable.

hints: How many things should change between runs?
Think about the generator: one fixed mesh.

prompt: The energy has settled at 450 eV but the pressure is still changing. You plan a cell relaxation. What follows?

options.text: Use a higher ENCUT; stress converges more slowly than energy
options.why: This is Pulay stress; a relaxation that changes volume needs at least 1.3 times ENMAX.

options.text: 450 eV is fine because the energy is converged
options.why: Tempting, but the stress is what drives a volume change.

options.text: Lower ENCUT to speed up the relaxation
options.why: Tempting for speed, but it makes the stress worse.

hints: Which quantity drives the cell change?
Stress versus energy convergence.

prompt: Put the ENCUT test in order.

options.text: Read the largest ENMAX from the POTCARs
options.why: Step 1: it sets the starting value.

options.text: Generate the runs that differ only in ENCUT
options.why: Step 2: one folder per value.

options.text: Run them all and collect the energies
options.why: Step 3: collect.sh writes the CSV.

options.text: Plot energy per atom against ENCUT
options.why: Step 4: the plotter marks the tolerance band.

options.text: Pick the cheapest setting that has stopped changing
options.why: Step 5: the decision.

hints: You need the numbers before the plot.
The decision is last.

prompt: Why do metals need a denser k-mesh than insulators?

options.text: The Fermi surface makes occupations jump inside the zone
options.why: The sum over points then converges slowly.
Tempting, but the cell size is not the reason.
Tempting, but ENCUT is a different setting.

hints: Think about filled versus partly filled bands.
Where does the occupation change abruptly?

prompt: In the Field Handbook's example series 4x4x4, 6x6x6, 8x8x8, when do you stop refining?

options.text: When the energy changes by less than about 1 meV per atom
options.why: That is the handbook tolerance for the energy.
Tempting because the example has three, but the stopping rule is the tolerance.

options.text: When the run takes more than an hour
options.why: Tempting, but cost is not a convergence criterion.

hints: What number did the handbook give?
Convergence is about the result, not the count.

prompt: Which centring keeps the lattice symmetry for every cell type?

options.why: It always keeps the symmetry of the lattice.
Tempting, but it can break the symmetry of hexagonal and fcc-primitive cells.

options.text: A mesh shifted by half a step on every axis
options.why: Tempting, but a shifted mesh is the typical cause of the IBZKPT error on hexagonal cells.

hints: Which centring never shifts the points off the origin?
Hexagonal cells are the classic problem.

prompt: For a metal you widen SIGMA until the mesh looks converged. What is the risk?

options.text: The energy drifts away from the zero-smearing value
options.why: Check the entropy term; keep |T*S| per atom small.
Tempting, but a wide SIGMA is allowed; it is just physically less accurate.
Tempting, but the mesh is set in KPOINTS, not by SIGMA.

hints: What does the entropy term measure?
Which energy do you quote?

prompt: With a doubled mesh along each of the three directions, roughly how many times more k-points are there before symmetry is used?
hints: Two times along x, y and z.

prompt: An ionic step ends at NELM. What does VASP do next, and what does that mean for the forces?

options.text: It continues anyway; the forces of that step are unreliable
options.why: VASP does not stop, so you must check OSZICAR.
Tempting, but VASP only shows the problem in the files.
Tempting, but NELM is a fixed limit.

hints: Does VASP report this as an error?
What do you look at to notice it?

prompt: Put the first fixes for a loop that will not converge in the handbook order.

options.text: Check the structure for overlapping atoms
options.why: First: most "unconvergeable" cases are broken geometries.

options.text: Use ALGO = All and raise NELM
options.why: Second: a more robust algorithm and more steps.
Third: gentler steps against sloshing.

options.text: Widen SIGMA a little for a metal
options.why: Fourth: softer occupations help the hard phase.
Fifth: when the highest bands are occupied.

hints: The cheapest check comes first.
Mixing comes after the algorithm.

prompt: What is charge sloshing?

options.text: The density swinging back and forth between steps instead of settling
options.why: Common in large cells, slabs and metals.
Tempting, but the cell is periodic and charge does not leave.

options.text: A rounding error in the energy
options.why: Tempting, but it is a feature of the iteration, not of rounding.

hints: Think of water in a tank.
Which column of OSZICAR shows it?

prompt: Which settings follow the handbook for linear mixing in a slab?

options.why: These soften the mixing; for magnets add AMIX_MAG = 0.4 and BMIX_MAG = 0.0001.
Tempting as "more mixing", but larger steps make sloshing worse.
Tempting, but that only limits the number of steps.

hints: Smaller numbers mean gentler mixing.
BMIX very small is linear mixing.

prompt: You only raise NELM from 60 to 300 and the loop still uses all steps. What is the right conclusion?

options.text: Something else is wrong; look at structure, algorithm and mixing
options.why: A larger NELM only hides the problem.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; slow convergence is normal
options.why: Tempting, but using every step means the loop is not converging.
Tempting as a shortcut, but a loose EDIFF stops the loop without real convergence.

hints: Is raising NELM a fix or a delay?
What did the page say about NELM alone?

prompt: You set NSW = 50 and no IBRION. OSZICAR shows temperatures T=. What happened?

options.text: IBRION defaulted to 0, which is molecular dynamics
options.why: Always set IBRION explicitly in a relaxation INCAR.
Tempting, but a relaxation does not print a temperature.
Tempting, but the T= is the ionic temperature of an MD run.

hints: What is the default IBRION?
Which run type prints T=?

prompt: ZBRENT: fatal error in bracketing. Which is a first step?

options.text: Copy CONTCAR to POSCAR and restart, tightening EDIFF
options.why: Often the structure is already near the minimum.
Tempting for a fresh start, but VASP needs it.
Tempting, but the line search failure is not about the step count.

hints: Is the structure perhaps already close to converged?
Which file holds the last structure?

prompt: Your slab relaxed with ISIF = 3 and the vacuum layer is gone. Why?

options.text: The vacuum has no stress to resist the cell shrinking
options.why: Use ISIF = 2 for slabs, surfaces and molecules in a box.
Tempting, but the cause is the cell relaxation, not the step size.
Tempting, but ENCUT does not remove vacuum.

hints: Which ISIF changes the cell?
What resists compression in empty space?

prompt: A volume relaxation changes the cell again when you rerun it from CONTCAR. What is the likely cause and cure?

options.text: Pulay stress; use about 1.3 times the largest ENMAX and rerun until the volume stops changing
options.why: Finish with a static run on the final structure.
Tempting, but the file is correct; the basis is tied to the starting cell.
Tempting, but k-points are not the cause of a drifting volume.

hints: Which quantity is biased when the basis is fixed?
How many rounds are normal?

prompt: With EDIFFG = -0.01, when does the relaxation stop?

options.text: When the largest force is below 0.01 eV per angstrom
options.why: A negative EDIFFG is a force criterion.

options.text: When the energy changes by less than 0.01 eV
options.why: Tempting, but that is what a positive EDIFFG means.
Tempting, but EDIFFG is not a time.

hints: Look at the sign.
Forces are in eV per angstrom.

prompt: Where does VASP print its error messages?

options.text: To standard output (your job log), not to OUTCAR
options.why: Read the end of vasp.out or the scheduler log first.
Tempting, but OUTCAR often ends without an explanation.
Tempting, but VASP writes no such file.

hints: Which file is your scheduler writing?
OUTCAR is not the first place.

prompt: Put the first three looks in order after a crash.

options.why: First: the error text.
Second: electronic loop or ionic step.
Third: the last thing VASP did.

hints: Start with the text of the error.
OUTCAR is the longest.

prompt: The job disappeared with no message at all. What is the usual cause?

options.text: The wall-time limit or running out of memory
options.why: Check the scheduler log.
Tempting, but a bad INCAR normally prints a message.
Tempting, but that gives a warning or error text.

hints: Who stops a job silently?
Where is that logged?

prompt: Your log has two errors, one early and one late. Which do you fix first?

options.why: One real failure often triggers a cascade.
Tempting because it is at the bottom, but it may be a consequence.
Tempting, but it wastes reruns when the first is the real cause.

hints: What causes what?
Read in the order things happened.

prompt: The error finder matches your pasted text only on keywords, not on an exact message. How should you treat the result?

options.text: As a suggestion to check; look for the exact message to confirm
options.why: Exact and routine-name matches are stronger evidence.

options.text: As certain, because the finder is automatic
options.why: Tempting, but keyword matches are only possible matches.

options.text: As wrong, because it is not exact
options.why: Tempting, but keyword matches are often useful; they just need checking.

hints: Which match kind is the weakest?
What would make you sure?
